Los Angeles, California · bring the bike

Should you bring your bike to Los Angeles?

Bring it.

The short answer, in full

Alaska, Southwest, Delta and American all check a packed bike as a standard bag, so it costs the same as your suitcase, $45 each way (Sept 2026), and Bike Shop LA in West Hollywood receives a BikeFlights delivery and builds it if you would rather not fly with the case. Renting only wins on a one- or two-day trip: the two Westside road rentals run $50 to $120 a day (Sept 2026), and nobody rents gravel. You will want a car; the coast, the canyons and the San Gabriels start 20 to 40 miles apart.

Fly itShip itRent oneGet aroundThe rules

Flying to Los Angeles with a bike

  1. Los Angeles International (LAX)

    • 12 mi from Los Angeles

    About 12 miles southwest of downtown and the closest airport to the Westside riding.

    More about LAX

    Alaska (Terminal 6), Southwest (Terminal 1), Delta (Terminal 3), American (Terminal 4) and United (Terminal 7), per the airport’s airline list (Sept 2026). Ride apps and taxis pick up at the LAX-it lot next to Terminal 1, a walk or a free shuttle from the terminals; rental car offices are off airport by shuttle.

  2. Hollywood Burbank (BUR)

    • 12 mi from Los Angeles

    About 12 miles north of downtown.

    More about BUR

    The airport for Griffith Park, the Valley and the Pasadena side. Alaska, American, Delta, Frontier, JetBlue, Southwest, Spirit and United, per the airport’s FAQ (Sept 2026). Ten on-site rental car companies in one building, and an Amtrak and Metrolink station across the street. Smaller and faster to get out of than LAX.

  3. Long Beach (LGB)

    • 17 mi from Los Angeles

    About 17 miles south of downtown.

    More about LGB

    The airport for the South Bay, Palos Verdes and the Long Beach rides. Southwest, Hawaiian, Delta and Alaska, per the airport’s airlines page (Sept 2026). Small; a Southwest rider from Phoenix or Boise lands here without the LAX crowd.

  4. Ontario International (ONT)

    • 37 mi from Los Angeles

    About 37 miles east of downtown, on the far side of the San Gabriels’ foothills.

    More about ONT

    Closer to Glendora Mountain Road than to anything on the coast. Alaska, American, Delta, Frontier, JetBlue, Southwest, United and others, per the airport’s airlines page (Sept 2026). Only worth it for a GMR or Mt. Baldy trip.

  5. John Wayne (Orange County) (SNA)

    • 34 mi from Los Angeles

    About 34 miles southeast of downtown, in Orange County.

    More about SNA

    Alaska, American, Delta, Southwest, United, Frontier, Spirit and others, per the airport’s airlines page (Sept 2026). Wrong side of the metro for the Westside, the canyons and the San Gabriels; a fallback fare, not a plan.

What the airlines charge

Read on each airline’s own page, Sept 2026.

Airline by airline

Alaska: a non-motorized bike in a soft or hard case or the maker’s box is a standard checked bag; the oversize fee is waived and the overweight fee is waived up to 70 lb; over 115 linear inches pays oversize, over 70 lb pays overweight; one bike per case, handlebars sideways, pedals off. First bag $45, second $55 for flights ticketed on or after April 10, 2026. Southwest: a non-motorized single-seat bike is checked baggage at the standard bag fee with oversize fees waived; over 100 lb or 115 linear inches is refused; pedals and handlebars removed and wrapped; a cardboard or soft case flies with a limited release. First bag $45, second $55 for travel booked on or after April 9, 2026 ($35 and $45 before). Delta: a non-motorized touring or single-seat racing bike in a container built for bikes goes at the standard bag allowance and fee; over 50 lb pays the excess weight fee; over 115 linear inches or 100 lb is refused; soft bags sign a limited release. First bag $45, second $55, US domestic Main. American: one non-motorized bike in a hard case, bike bag or box; standard checked bag fee up to 50 lb, standard overweight fee 51 to 70 lb, oversize fees do not apply; handlebars fixed sideways and pedals off or wrapped; not in a hard case it is treated as fragile. First bag $50 ($45 paid online), second $60 ($55 online), updated May 18, 2026. United: not confirmed; check its sports-equipment page before you book. Keep a bike case under 50 lb on every one of these and it is one ordinary checked bag.

Shipping your bike to Los Angeles

One shop says it on its own site: Bike Shop LA in West Hollywood takes BikeFlights deliveries addressed to the shop and builds the bike.

How shipping works here

No build fee is published (Sept 2026). Helen’s Cycles, Bike Attack and Incycle each publish a fee to assemble a boxed bike ($145, $120 to $300 and $70 to $200, Sept 2026) but none says it will receive a shipment — call before you book. Bike Shop LA’s page says BikeFlights typically runs about $100 within the US (Sept 2026). BikeFlights ships by UPS and tells you to allow an extra day or two for weather; its pages do not state a transit-day count (read Sept 2026). ShipBikes, also UPS ground, says no more than 6 business days one way anywhere in the continental US (read Sept 2026). Ship a week ahead and the bike is built before you land.

  1. Bike Shop LA

    Register with BikeFlights, pick Bike Shop LA as the recipient.

    Website
    More about Bike Shop LA

    They build it and call when it is ready. Build fee not published (Sept 2026). Open every day. 7740 Santa Monica Blvd, West Hollywood; (323) 515-0070.

Renting a bike in Los Angeles

Two Westside shops rent a road bike worth the day.

What renting costs and what you get

Neither lists sizes, so call with your height. Helen’s Cycles Santa Monica has a carbon Cannondale SuperSix EVO CRB 3 at $120 a day, $90 a day for three days, $75 a day for five or more, with the pedals you ask for (Sept 2026). Bike Attack on Main Street has Bianchi and KHS road bikes at Shimano 105 level, $50 a day or $75 for 24 hours, first come first served (Sept 2026). No gravel or mountain bike rental was confirmed anywhere. Helen’s Manhattan Beach rents only a Treadwell fitness bike, $50 a day (Sept 2026), which does the beach path and not much more. The math: flying the bike costs $90 round trip on Alaska, Southwest or Delta and $100 on American (Sept 2026), so renting wins only on a one- or two-day trip, and only if a 105-level bike in a size you did not choose is fine for the Donut (Saturdays, 8:00 am) or Latigo. Three days or more, bring yours. Gravel: bring yours, nobody rents one.

  1. Helen’s Cycles Santa Monica

    Cannondale SuperSix EVO CRB 3 (carbon road). $120 one day, $90 a day for three days, $75 a day for five or more (Sept 2026).

    Website
    More about Helen’s Cycles Santa Monica

    Pedals, helmet and lock free on request; flat kit included; photo ID. Reserve ahead: (310) 829-1836. Sizes not listed. Closed Mondays.

  2. Bike Attack

    Bianchi and KHS road bikes, Shimano 105 or similar. $50 a day or $75 for 24 hours (Sept 2026).

    Website
    More about Bike Attack

    First come first served, no reservations; call (310) 862-5001 for availability. Waiver, ID and card copy. Sizes not listed. Open every day 10 to 6.

Getting around Los Angeles with a bike

You’ll want a car.

Getting around, in full

Yes, unless you are staying on the Westside and riding only the coast and La Grange’s Nichols Canyon ride (Sundays, 8:00 am). The zones sit far apart: the Westwood ride start is about 11 miles from downtown, Pasadena and the San Gabriels are about 18 miles the other way, Glendora Mountain Road is another 20 beyond that, and the canyon climbs start in Malibu. Out of LAX with a bike case: rental car offices are off airport, reached by the free shuttle under the purple Rental Car sign; ride apps and taxis pick up at the LAX-it lot next to Terminal 1, a walk or a free shuttle from the terminals (the airport’s ground-transport page, Sept 2026) — book an XL and expect the case to ride in the back. The FlyAway bus runs nonstop to Union Station and Van Nuys, $12.75 one way, contactless card or app only; its pages say nothing about oversize luggage or bike boxes. Metro rail from LAX: a free shuttle from the terminals to the LAX/Metro Transit Center for the C and K Lines, $1.75 a ride with free transfers for two hours (metro.net, Sept 2026); fine with a built bike, not the way to move a case.

  • Transit: LA Metro, read Sept 2026: bikes ride on rail at all operating hours.
  • Bike share: Metro Bike Share
Transit and bike share, in full

Transit: LA Metro, read Sept 2026: bikes ride on rail at all operating hours; board at the doors marked with the yellow bike sign and stand with the bike in the open area. E-bikes are allowed on trains if they are standard-bike sized and pass inspection; fuel-powered, three-wheeled, tandem, recumbent and over-six-foot bikes, mopeds and trailers are not. Every bus has two or more racks on the front; motorized bikes and any bike over 55 lb cannot go on the rack; folding bikes with wheels 20 inches or smaller ride inside. Metrolink (Burbank airport station, Union Station) has its own bike rules on metrolinktrains.com; not read this run.

Bike share: Classic and electric bikes, 24 hours. A single ride is $1.75 per 30 minutes; an e-bike is $1 more to unlock for casual riders (Sept 2026). Docks are downtown, on the Westside and along the river path, not in the canyons. For the errand or the ride to dinner, not the ride.

The rules on the road in California

California, read Sept 2026.

Every rule, in full

Drivers must give three feet when passing a bike (Vehicle Code 21760, the Three Feet for Safety Act); since January 1, 2023 (AB 1909) a driver in the same lane must change lanes to pass when one is open, and when three feet is not possible must slow to a reasonable speed and pass only when it does not endanger the rider. The fine is $35, $220 if a collision injures the rider. Helmets are required under 18 (21212). E-bikes come in three classes (312.5): class 1 pedal-assist to 20 mph, class 2 throttle to 20 mph, class 3 pedal-assist to 28 mph with a speedometer, rider 16 or older and helmeted. Ride as far right as practicable except when passing, turning left, avoiding a hazard or in a lane too narrow to share (21202). Sidewalk riding is set city by city (21206); the City of Los Angeles allows it unless ridden with willful or wanton disregard for people or property (LAMC 56.15), and Santa Monica and the beach cities set their own rules. California has no stop-as-yield law. The read: the city recorded 303 traffic deaths in 2024 by preliminary LAPD data, up from about 240 when Vision Zero began in 2015, and the city controller’s April 2025 audit said the program was hampered by weak political support and half its projects unbuilt (LAist, April 14, 2025). LAPD data through late 2024 put 35 percent of fatal crashes as hit-and-runs and most bicycling deaths in South LA (BikinginLA, Oct 2024; Crosstown, Nov 2024). The coast path and the canyon roads are a different world from the boulevards; the miles between them are where you stay alert.
